Threat.value: Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen
I feel on guard even inside my own home
I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me

Memory.value: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me
The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to
When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop

Negative Appraisals.value: My reactions since the event mean that I am going crazy
The world is a dangerous place
I can't stop bad things from happening to me

issues.explanation: 'Risky Behavior' is poorly integrated with the rest of the profile. The other threat items reflect hypervigilance and perceived danger (silence, being on guard at home), while memory and appraisal items center on intrusive, overwhelming captivity memories and beliefs that the world is dangerous or that she is 'going crazy.' Risk-taking points toward a different behavioral pattern that is not supported elsewhere, especially with Maladaptive Strategies absent and Threat not strongly linked outward in the formulation.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Life Not Worth Living
issues.explanation: 'Life Not Worth Living' is difficult to reconcile with the rest of the selected appraisals, which otherwise focus on danger and loss of control ('world is dangerous,' 'going crazy'). It introduces a severe hopelessness/suicidal cognition not echoed in memory, threat, or strategy items. At PCL-5 53 severe symptoms are plausible, but this specific appraisal is insufficiently supported by the rest of the profile and feels clinically disconnected rather than integrated.

vignette: Maria, a 66‑year‑old paramedic who has spent the past four decades answering the call in the streets of San Luis, remembers the night that changed her life like a photograph taken in a flash that never fades. While responding to a collapsed patient on a quiet corner of the city, she was suddenly seized by masked men and dragged into a narrow alley that led to a small warehouse. The room was dim and the air thick with the metallic scent of sweat and fear. She was bound, her head tilted, the world reduced to the muffled hum of a single bulb and the silence that pressed against her ears. When the captors finally released her, she emerged bruised, bewildered, and terrified of the dark. The terror that flooded her mind after that night left Maria convinced she was “going crazy.” She told her husband that the memories felt unreal, that the story was too extreme to be true. That conviction made her look for ways the world could be dangerous and helpless. She began to believe that her own mind was betraying her, that every sudden noise, every shadow, could signal another kidnapping. These fears shaped how she replayed the event in her head: the silence as a prelude to danger, the feeling of helplessness as a promise that something worse might follow. Whenever Maria hears an unusual silence—such as the stillness inside a paramedic box during a long drive or the quiet hum of a city at night—her mind reverts to that warehouse. She sees the silence as a threat and feels a surge of panic. The memory flashes back in vivid detail: the muffled sounds of the captors, the cold air against her skin, the sense that every breath could be her last. That intrusive recall forces her to check behind her, to keep alert even in the safe confines of her own home. The connection between the memory and the threat she feels becomes almost automatic, like a muscle memory. At the same time, each time that flash of the warehouse returns, Maria’s belief that the world is a dangerous place deepens. She interprets the memory as proof that the universe is hostile and that she is powerless to stop it. The memory’s relentless intrusion feeds her sense of helplessness, convincing her that she cannot control what will happen next. It is as if the story itself becomes a prophecy, telling her that danger is always near and that she is doomed to live in constant fear. In the weeks that followed, Maria began to alter her routines. She refused night shifts, citing the fear of walking home alone after the dark shift. She kept her phone at the ready, constantly checking it for messages from her husband or from the dispatcher. At the station, she kept a cautious distance from other paramedics, watching their movements, as if any sudden motion could mean an impending attack. The avoidance of darkness and the constant vigilance disrupted her work flow; she was late on several calls, her hesitation costing her precious minutes that could have saved a life. Her husband noticed her growing unease and the way she avoided looking directly at her reflection, as if she feared her own eyes might reveal the truth. Finally, the night her daughter’s voice rang through her cell phone—an ordinary call asking about dinner—brought Maria to her limits. She almost grabbed the receiver in a reflex of alertness, then froze when the phone was still. The panic was so intense that she stumbled out of the station, shaking, and found herself at the threshold of her apartment, breathing raggedly. It was then she decided to seek help. Maria’s biggest fear is that her fear will continue to consume her, that she will lose her job and her sense of safety. Her hope is that she can learn to calm the memory so that she can feel the silence of a night without hearing a threat.
